title: What 625,987 NHTSA complaints look like once you count them one way
author: Iqbal Taher
summary: Every car owner in the US can file a safety complaint with NHTSA, and every one of those complaints is public. The catch is the format. The flat file is about 1.6 GB of tab-separated text, one row per complaint per component , written for investigators rather than for anyone trying to answer a simple question like "which models draw the most complaints?" I wanted that answer for model years 2010 to 2025, and I wanted it in a form other people could check and cite. Here is what I learned turning the raw file into a small, citable dataset. One complaint, one vehicle, counted once The first trap is double counting. A single complaint can sit on several rows, because the owner ticked more than one component (say, "steering" and "electrical system"). If you count rows, a busy complaint looks like three. So the rule is simple and written down before any counting starts: Each complaint is counted once per make, model and model year , keyed on its complaint number. It is counted once per component it names, so component totals can add up to more than the vehicle total. Writing the rule first matters more than the code. It is what lets someone else rebuild the numbers and get the same result. Keep NHTSA's own names It is tempting to tidy model names that appear under several spellings, or merge sub-components. I didn't. Model names and components stay exactly as NHTSA records them. Merging feels cleaner, but every merge is a judgment call someone else can't reproduce. When I tested merging the common name variants anyway, none of the top 25 rows moved. Counts are not failure rates The file has no sales figures. A model that sold in huge numbers can collect more complaints than a rarer car with a worse record. That is the single most important caveat, so it goes in the dataset card, the report and the CSV notes, not in a footnote. What came out From the copy of the file dated August 25, 2026: 625,987 complaints across 4,087 make, model and model-year combinations. The 2010 Ford Fusion has the most of any vehicle, 5,126, with steering named most. Ford holds 17 of the 25 most complained-about vehicles. The only vehicle from model year 2023 or newer in the top 100 is the 2023 Tesla Model Y. Making it citable A dataset nobody can cite is a dataset nobody uses. So the CSV (one row per make, model, model year and component, 90,254 rows), a JSON summary and the build script are archived on Zenodo with a DOI (10.5281/zenodo.23685716), and mirrored on GitHub, Hugging Face and Kaggle under CC BY 4.0. Each edition stays frozen at its own address, so a number quoted today still points to the same number next year. If you want the charts, the full ranking and the method written out for non-developers, the write-up is here: the most complained-about cars ranked by NHTSA complaints . I'm Iqbal Taher. I write for Oil & Miles , where we turn federal car records into plain-English guides.

title: Integrating YOLO Fire Detection with FastAPI and Next.js 🔥
author: Abdullah Javed
summary: A practical walkthrough of setting up FlameGuard, connecting a custom YOLO model, and debugging a full-stack Computer Vision application. Introduction I recently explored FlameGuard , an open-source fire detection application built with YOLO, FastAPI, and Next.js. I wanted to understand how a trained object detection model works inside a complete web application. I used the original FlameGuard repository and adapted it to work with my own trained fire detection model. Here's a breakdown of the implementation and what I learned. Tech Stack Technology Purpose Python Backend development YOLO Fire detection OpenCV Image processing FastAPI REST API SQLite Detection history Next.js Frontend React User interface Conda Dependency management 1. Project Setup Clone the repository: git clone https://github.com/nohsangwoo/FlameGuard.git cd FlameGuard The main project structure is: FlameGuard/ ├── backend/ │ ├── app/ │ └── environment.yml ├── frontend/ └── README.md Create the Python environment: cd backend conda env create -f environment.yml conda activate flameguard 2. Integrating the YOLO Model I already had a trained fire detection model named best.pt . The model contains one detection class: { 0 : " fire " } I placed the model in the backend's assets directory and configured the detection endpoint to use it. from pathlib import Path from ultralytics import YOLO APP_DIR = Path ( __file__ ). resolve (). parents [ 2 ] MODEL_PATH = APP_DIR / " assets " / " best.pt " model = YOLO ( str ( MODEL_PATH )) Loading the model outside the API handler avoids repeatedly initializing it for each request. 3. Running Fire Detection The prediction process uses the YOLO model to analyze an uploaded image. results = model . predict ( source = str ( temp_file_path ), conf = 0.25 , imgsz = 640 ) result = results [ 0 ] We can extract detection information: for box in result . boxes : class_id = int ( box . cls . item ()) class_name = model . names [ class_id ] confidence = float ( box . conf . item ()) bbox = box . xyxy [ 0 ]. tolist () print ( class_name , confidence , bbox ) Each detection includes a predicted class, confidence score, and bounding-box coordinates. 4. Creating Annotated Images Ultralytics provides a convenient method for drawing predicted bounding boxes: annotated_img = result . plot () The annotated image can then be saved using OpenCV: import cv2 cv2 . imwrite ( str ( log_file_path ), annotated_img ) These images can be used by the frontend to display detection results. 5. FastAPI Integration The backend exposes a prediction endpoint: POST /predict_fire It receives an uploaded image, processes it with YOLO, and returns a structured detection response. For example, one of my tests returned: { "message" : "fire detected" , "file_name" : "frame.jpg" , "detections" : [ { "class_name" : "fire" , "confidence" : 0.419 } ] } The API can also store detection information in SQLite for later retrieval. 6. Debugging Detection Images One issue I encountered was that the backend returned successful predictions, but detection images were missing. The logs showed: POST /predict_fire 200 OK GET /log/image.jpg 404 Not Found I investigated the image-saving and static-file directory paths. Using pathlib helped keep the paths consistent: from pathlib import Path APP_DIR = Path ( __file__ ). resolve (). parents [ 2 ] LOG_DIR = APP_DIR / " log " LOG_DIR . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) This was a useful lesson in handling generated files inside FastAPI applications. 7. Running the Backend From the backend directory: python -m uvicorn app.main:app --reload The backend runs at: http://localhost:8000 API documentation: http://localhost:8000/docs 8. Running the Next.js Frontend Open another terminal: cd frontend pnpm install pnpm run dev The frontend runs at: http://localhost:3000 The interface communicates with the FastAPI backend to process images and retrieve detection results. 9. Handling Camera Errors During testing, I encountered a browser error related to: navigator . mediaDevices . enumerateDevices () A simple feature check helps prevent the application from crashing when the browser camera API is unavailable: if ( ! navigator . mediaDevices ?. enumerateDevices ) { console . warn ( " Camera API unavailable " ); return ; } const devices = await navigator . mediaDevices . enumerateDevices (); Browser permissions and secure-context requirements are important when working with camera-based applications. 10. Lessons Learned This project helped me better understand: YOLO inference and detection results. FastAPI integration with Computer Vision models. Image annotation and file management. SQLite detection logging. Next.js and backend communication. Debugging missing images and browser camera errors. Organizing a full-stack AI application. Future Improvements I plan to explore better detection accuracy, improve frontend interactions, test more challenging images, and make the application more reliable for continuous monitoring. The current project is a learning experiment rather than a production-ready fire safety system. Conclusion Working on FlameGuard was a valuable opportunity to connect Computer Vision concepts with full-stack application development. It also reminded me that a trained AI model is only one part of a complete application. There is much more to explore, and I look forward to improving my understanding through more practical projects. Original project: FlameGuard by nohsangwoo GitHub: github.com/abdullahjave Thanks for reading!

title: Replacing a Spreadsheet Report With an Automated Workflow: A Practical Checklist
author: Affix Center Softech Services Pvt. Ltd
summary: Most automation projects in a business do not start with a data lake. They start with a spreadsheet that someone rebuilds every Monday, a reconciliation between two exports, or a report that only one person knows how to make. Turning that into a reliable workflow is mostly about the boring parts: validation, exceptions and triggers. 1. Decide if the task is worth automating A simple filter works well. Automate when the task is: Frequent : daily or weekly, not a few times a year Structured : clear rules, inputs in a predictable shape Manual today : data entry, reconciliation or report generation done by hand If it fails one of these, fix the process before writing code. 2. Start from the data you already have Inventory the spreadsheets and applications the report currently pulls from Check their quality before building anything on top of them Consolidate sources into one pipeline (ETL or ELT) instead of copying cells between files Write down which department owns each source, because siloed data is usually the real problem 3. Build validation and exception handling in from day one Validate every input against explicit rules, so differences between teams are caught early Route bad records to an exception queue that a person reviews, instead of failing silently or passing them through Log what ran, when and with what inputs, so an audit-ready report can be traced back 4. Choose how runs are triggered Rule-based or scheduled for fixed reporting cycles Event-driven / trigger-based when a file lands or a record changes in another system Keep orchestration in one place so a multi-system flow is visible end to end 5. Deliver to the right reader Role-based dashboards or reports, so each person sees only what they need Management or MIS views for leadership, operational views for field teams Restrict access to dashboards, reports and models by role More detail: data analytics and intelligent workflow automation at Affix Center Written by the team at Affix Center , an IT services company in Lower Parel, Mumbai.

title: 5 Security Holes Almost Every AI Generated App Ships With (And How to Fix Them)
author: Alon Trifonov
summary: AI app builders like Lovable, Bolt, and v0 are impressive. You describe what you want, wait a few minutes, and get a working app that looks ready for real users. It is not ready for real users. I'm Alon Trifonov, founder of Zyntari, a small engineering studio in Israel. A big part of my job is taking AI-generated prototypes and turning them into production software, mostly Python and Flask on the backend. After auditing a bunch of these apps, I keep finding the same five security holes. Not exotic, movie-hacker stuff. The boring classics: the kind that show up in the OWASP Top 10 year after year because developers keep making the same mistakes. Now AI generators are making those same mistakes at scale. Every one of them is fixable in under an hour. Here is what to look for, how to check if your app has the problem, and exactly how to fix it. 1. Debug mode left on Open the main file of your generated app. If you see this, you have a problem: if name == " main ": app.run(debug=True) Why it's dangerous: debug=True enables the Werkzeug debugger, an interactive Python console that runs in your browser. If it ever reaches a live server, anyone who triggers an error in your app gets a console that can run arbitrary code on your machine. The Werkzeug documentation says it in plain words: "the debugger must never be used on production machines." This is not a theoretical risk. In 2015, Patreon, a company with millions of users, left the Werkzeug debugger publicly accessible. Security researchers at Detectify warned them about it, and days later attackers walked in through exactly that hole and dumped 15 gigabytes of user data online, including 2.3 million email addresses. How to check: search your whole codebase for "debug". Every match should end up controlled by the environment, never hardcoded. The fix: import os if name == " main ": app.run(debug=os.environ.get("FLASK_DEBUG", "false").lower() == "true") And in production, don't use Flask's built-in server at all. Use Gunicorn: gunicorn -w 4 -b 0.0.0.0:8000 "app:create_app()" 2. Secrets sitting directly in the code Generated code loves this pattern: app.secret_key = "super-secret-key-123" STRIPE_API_KEY = "sk_live_..." Why it's dangerous: anything committed to a Git repository should be treated as public. Yes, even in a private repo, because repos get shared, cloned, screenshotted, and pushed by accident. GitGuardian scans every public commit on GitHub, and their State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 report found 28.65 million new hardcoded secrets pushed to public GitHub in 2025 alone, up 34% year over year. Worse for us specifically: AI-assisted commits leaked secrets at roughly double the baseline rate. How to check: grep -rInE "(secret|api[_-]?key|password|token)\s*=\s*[\"']" . --include="*.py" If that command prints anything that looks like a real value, that is your to-do list. The fix: secrets come from the environment, never from source code: import os app.secret_key = os.environ.get("SECRET_KEY") if not app.secret_key: raise RuntimeError("SECRET_KEY is not set. Refusing to start insecurely.") Generate a proper key: python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))" Then set it wherever you deploy. Render, Railway, and Docker all have an environment variables section for exactly this. And if a secret already leaked: rotate it. Deleting the commit does nothing. The value already lives in the repo history and in every scanner's database. 3. SQL injection hiding in "dynamic" queries Generators usually do the right thing and use an ORM like SQLAlchemy. The trouble starts when the AI needs something "dynamic," like a search filter, and reaches for string formatting: email = request.args.get("email") query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'" result = db.session.execute(query) Why it's dangerous: that f-string is a door directly into your database. A user who types ' OR '1'='1' -- as their email just bypassed your login. Injection has been in the top three of the OWASP Top 10 for over two decades, precisely because one formatted string is all it takes. How to check: search for f", %, or .format( on the same line as execute(. Any hit is a red flag. The fix: pass values as parameters and let the driver escape them: from sqlalchemy import text email = request.args.get("email", "") result = db.session.execute( text("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = :email"), {"email": email}, ) Or stay fully in the ORM, which is even simpler: user = User.query.filter_by(email=email).first() Rule of thumb: if you ever see an f-string inside a database query in AI-generated code, review the entire file. Where there is one, there are usually more. 4. Login endpoints anyone can hammer forever A typical generated login route looks fine: @app.route("/api/login", methods=["POST"]) def login(): user = User.query.filter_by(email=request.json["email"]).first() if user and check_password(request.json["password"], user.password_hash): return jsonify(token=create_token(user)) return jsonify(error="invalid credentials"), 401 The problem is what it doesn't do: it lets anyone try passwords as fast as their machine can send requests. No limit, no slowdown, no lockout. Weak passwords fall in hours. How to check: look at your login endpoint and ask a simple question. What stops someone from sending ten thousand requests? If the answer is "nothing," that is the hole. The fix: rate limit the sensitive endpoints. Flask-Limiter makes it a two-line change: from flask_limiter import Limiter from flask_limiter.util import get_remote_address limiter = Limiter(get_remote_address, app=app, storage_uri="redis://localhost:6379") @app.route("/api/login", methods=["POST"]) @limiter.limit("5 per minute") def login(): ... Five attempts per minute per IP turns "try a million passwords tonight" into "try a few thousand over days." Most attackers just move on. Do the same for registration, password reset, and any endpoint that sends emails or SMS. Those are abuse magnets too. And make sure passwords are stored with bcrypt or argon2, via Werkzeug's generate_password_hash, never plain text or fast hashes like MD5. 5. No security headers at all Open your browser's developer tools, go to the Network tab, and click any response from your app. If you don't see headers like Content-Security-Policy or Strict-Transport-Security, your app is telling browsers "trust everything, embed me anywhere." Why it's dangerous: without a Content-Security-Policy, one reflected XSS, meaning a malicious script sneaked in through user input or a crafted link, runs with full access to your users' sessions. Without X-Frame-Options, an attacker can embed your app inside their own page and trick users into clicking things they can't see. That is clickjacking. Flask deliberately does not set these headers for you, and generators quietly skip the step. The fix: one extension, about ten lines: from flask_talisman import Talisman Talisman( app, content_security_policy={ "default-src": "'self'", "script-src": "'self'", "style-src": "'self'", }, force_https=False, # let your reverse proxy (Nginx/Cloudflare) handle HTTPS ) If your app legitimately needs external scripts like analytics or payment widgets, add those specific domains to the policy instead of disabling it. The bigger picture None of this is really the AI's fault. Generators optimize for "does it run and does it look right." Security is invisible until the day it fails, so it gets skipped by default. Every generated app needs one deliberate hardening pass before real users and real data touch it. One hour, one checklist: No debug=True anywhere near production No secrets in code. Environment variables only, and rotate anything that ever leaked No f-strings or string formatting inside database queries Rate limits on login, registration, and reset endpoints Security headers via Flask-Talisman Bonus: passwords hashed with bcrypt or argon2, and dependencies scanned regularly My rule of thumb, and the mindset behind everything we ship at Zyntari: treat AI-generated code like code from a fast, talented junior developer who has never been on call during a breach. A great starting point, never the finished product. Review the auth, review the queries, review the secrets. Then ship. Alon Trifonov is the founder of Zyntari (zyntari.com), an independent engineering studio in Israel that turns prototypes and AI-generated apps into secure, production-grade software. He builds with Python, Flask, and React, with security as a default rather than an afterthought.

title: Scans, Sideways Pages and Readable Garbage: Why an AI Agent Misses Half a PDF
author: Devaland
summary: On 24 August my AI agent read a 29-page tender document and told me that two required sections were missing: the invitation and the technical specification. We wrote to the institution to say their published documentation was incomplete. They answered politely that it was in the attached documents. They were right. Pages 1 to 12 of that PDF were scans: photographs of paper at 300 dots per inch, with no text layer at all. The text extractor returned nothing for them, without an error. The agent read the 17 pages that had text, saw no invitation and no specification there, and reported what it had seen as the whole document. Coverage was 59 percent. Nothing measured it, so it read as 100. An empty page is a question A PDF can carry text in two ways. A document exported from a word processor has a text layer, and extraction is exact. A scanned document is a stack of pictures, and the only way to read it is optical character recognition, OCR, which is slow, approximate and easy to forget. The extractor does not tell you which kind of page it got. It returns an empty string for a scan and an empty string for a blank page, and both look like "nothing here". So the first check is per page, before any conclusion about the document: import subprocess def text_per_page ( pdf , pages ): out = [] for n in range ( 1 , pages + 1 ): t = subprocess . run ([ " pdftotext " , " -f " , str ( n ), " -l " , str ( n ), pdf , " - " ], capture_output = True , text = True ). stdout out . append ( t ) return out def unread_pages ( texts , min_chars = 40 ): return [ n for n , t in enumerate ( texts , 1 ) if len ( t . strip ()) < min_chars ] If unread_pages is not empty, the document has not been read. Those pages go to OCR, and until they come back, the only honest answer is "could not check", with the page numbers. My reader now prints the character count for every page, OCRs the empty ones at 300 dpi, and exits with an error while any page is still unread. Its last line is === READ COMPLETE === . No sentinel, no conclusion. Readable garbage OCR does not fail loudly either. It returns text, and the text can be nonsense. On 7 September the agent read a 14-page reply from a public institution. Every page was a scan, every page went through OCR, and the reader printed READ COMPLETE. Four of the pages were printed in landscape, a wide table turned sideways on the sheet. OCR read them upright and produced fragments of columns: real letters, real-looking words, no meaning. The summary said "four planned positions". The document listed more than twenty-five awarded contracts. Character count cannot catch this. The garbage had plenty of characters. What it lacked was words. So the reader now measures that, crudely and cheaply: import re def readability ( text ): words = re . findall ( r " [^\W\d_]{3,} " , text ) if not words : return 0.0 real = [ w for w in words if re . search ( r " [aeiouAEIOU] " , w )] return len ( real ) / max ( 1 , len ( text . split ())) It is the share of tokens that look like words: three letters or more, with a vowel. It knows nothing about any language, and it does not need to. On those four pages the upright reading scored between 0.05 and 0.07. Rotated by 90 degrees, the same pages scored between 0.57 and 0.64. So when a page scores low, or is wider than it is tall, the reader OCRs it again at 90 and 270 degrees and keeps the best reading. It also says so, on its error output: "page 5 was sideways, rotated". A silent correction is how the next person never learns the document had sideways pages. The rotation is only tried when needed. OCR is the most expensive thing my server does, and turning every page three ways would triple the cost for all the pages that were already fine. The same thing happens with tables. The OCR engine has layout modes, and the one that treats the page as a single block of text destroys a table. On the same day, a procurement plan read in that mode came back as "no IT purchases"; the mode that looks for columns read the same image about ten times better. If a page is a table, the reading mode is part of the question. When two readings disagree Some things on a page matter more than the rest: a date, an amount, a reference number. OCR gets single digits wrong more often than words, because a word has redundancy and a digit has none. On the 24 August document, the deadline came back as 23.08 in one layout mode and as 28.08 in another. Same image, same engine. Neither reading announced any doubt. So when a digit matters, the reader runs more than one mode and compares: def digits_agree ( readings ): """ readings: the same line as read by several OCR modes. """ found = [ tuple ( re . findall ( r " \d+ " , r )) for r in readings ] return len ( set ( found )) == 1 If they agree, the value is probably right. If they disagree, the value is not known, and the agent does not pick one. It reports both, with the page, and the date comes from a source that is not a photograph: the published notice, the email, the person. The rule I wrote down after that day: OCR never settles a date. The read is not the answer There is one more way to lose a page, and it has nothing to do with OCR. On 26 August the agent read a six-page document correctly, every page, and then passed the output through head -120 to keep it short. The cut fell on page 4. It searched what was left for the figure the whole matter turned on, found nothing, and reported that the figure was not in the document. It was on page 6. The reader had done its job. The pipe threw the answer away, and what was left looked like a complete document. The fix was to stop searching outside the reader. Mine takes the search itself, --grep "pattern" , runs it over the complete text of every page, and prints either the matches with their page numbers or "0 matches over N of N pages: this is a true negative". It also writes the full text to a file and prints that path first, so even a truncated pipe leaves the complete text one step away. What the agent may conclude From a document where every page has text, or has been read by OCR with a readable score, and the sentinel was printed: what the document says. From a document with unread pages, low-scoring pages, or a digit two readings disagree on: nothing about those pages. It names them, and says what would settle them. From a slice of the output: nothing at all about the rest. Before you trust a reading of a document, count its pages, ask which ones were really read, and make the reader say so on its last line. This is a shortened version of chapter 6 of my book in progress, Agents You Can Leave Alone, which I am writing in public on Leanpub: https://leanpub.com/agents-you-can-leave-alone Originally published on devaland.com: Scans, Sideways Pages and Readable Garbage: Why an AI Agent Misses Half a PDF

title: Your Website Can Be Vulnerable Even When Your Code Looks Perfect
author: Deepak
summary: Many developers believe that secure code is enough to protect a website. Unfortunately, that is not always true. Your application also depends on its runtime, packages, plugins, server configuration, and third-party services. A vulnerability in one of these components can put the entire application at risk. The hidden risk behind dependencies Imagine building a website with PHP. Your own code validates user input, checks permissions, and protects database queries. But what happens if the PHP runtime or one of your dependencies contains a security vulnerability? Your application may still be exposed, even if you wrote your code carefully. Security is not just about the code you write. It is also about the software you trust. Why updating software matters Outdated software can contain publicly known vulnerabilities that attackers may try to exploit. Developers should regularly: Update supported PHP versions and security patches. Review Composer dependencies for known vulnerabilities. Remove unused packages and plugins. Monitor security advisories for their technology stack. Test updates before deploying them to production. Do not assume that installing a package once means it will remain secure forever. Three practical security checks for PHP developers Check your PHP version Run: php -v Check whether your version is still supported and whether your hosting environment has installed the latest applicable security patches. Audit Composer dependencies If your project uses Composer, run: composer audit This helps identify known security advisories affecting installed dependencies. Protect production configuration Never commit database passwords, API keys, or other secrets to a public repository. Use environment variables or an appropriate secrets-management system. Also, keep detailed error messages and debugging tools disabled in production. Security requires continuous attention A secure application is not something you build once and forget. New vulnerabilities are discovered, dependencies change, and software becomes outdated. Regular maintenance is part of responsible development. The best approach is simple: monitor, update, test, and verify. Final thoughts You do not need to be a cybersecurity expert to improve your application's security. Start by understanding the components your application depends on, checking them regularly, and fixing known issues promptly. One question for developers: How often do you audit the dependencies and runtime versions used by your production applications? Share your approach in the comments. I would love to learn what works for other developers.

title: 10 Companies Offering AI-Powered Mobile App Development Services in New York
author: David Johan
summary: Artificial intelligence is changing what businesses expect from their mobile apps. In New York, where startups and established companies compete for customer attention, features such as personalized recommendations, intelligent search, automated support, and predictive analytics are becoming increasingly useful. A mobile app can do more than display products or process transactions. It can help users find what they need faster, reduce repetitive work, and give businesses a clearer picture of customer behavior. For startups, even one well-executed AI feature can make a product more useful and distinctive. Larger organizations have a different opportunity: they can introduce machine learning, generative AI, or automation into existing applications without necessarily replacing their entire technology stack. The challenge is finding a development partner that understands both mobile engineering and the practical side of AI. A convincing demo is one thing. Building a secure, reliable application that people continue using is another. This guide looks at companies to consider when exploring AI-powered mobile app development, including their potential strengths and the kinds of projects they may suit. Whether you’re launching an MVP or adding intelligent features to an established product, the right choice starts with understanding what your business actually needs. 10 Companies Offering AI-Powered Mobile App Development Services in New York The best development partner isn’t necessarily the one offering the longest list of AI features. title: Content Security Policy Reporting: Two Silent CSP Blocks Nobody Noticed
author: NET_DARK_BOI
summary: A Content Security Policy (CSP) is a response header that tells the browser which scripts, styles, frames and connections a page may use. Anything outside the list is blocked. That is the point of CSP, and it is also its quietest failure mode: when a strict policy blocks something you wanted , the only trace is a line in the visitor's DevTools console. Your server sees nothing. Breachloom, a browser-based web security training site, runs a strict policy: script-src 'self' plus three named hosts, no inline scripts, no 'unsafe-inline' , no 'unsafe-eval' . Two things broke behind that policy, and both went unnoticed until violation reporting was switched on. Silent block #1: the analytics beacon that never loaded Cloudflare Web Analytics injects its beacon script into every HTML page served through Cloudflare. The beacon is loaded from static.cloudflareinsights.com and reports to cloudflareinsights.com . Neither host was in script-src or connect-src . Result: on every page view the browser blocked the beacon, logged a CSP error in the console and sent nothing. The analytics dashboard simply showed no data, which looks exactly like "no visitors" rather than "broken". The fix was two allow-list entries, kept as narrow as possible: script-src 'self' https://static.cloudflareinsights.com ... connect-src 'self' https://cloudflareinsights.com ... The lesson is not about Cloudflare. Any platform feature that injects a script (analytics, bot protection, a chat widget) is a new script source. If your policy is strict, the feature arrives already broken, and it fails silently. Silent block #2: a redirect that swapped the policy The site has an intentionally vulnerable page for its cross-site scripting exercises. That page must run a reflected payload, so it gets its own, separate policy: script-src 'unsafe-inline' , but also sandbox allow-scripts , connect-src 'none' , form-action 'none' and default-src 'none' . The sandbox gives the document an opaque ( null ) origin, so a payload that runs there cannot read the site's cookies or storage, or call its API. The special policy was attached by matching the path /ctf/xss-victim.html . On production, Cloudflare Pages normalises clean URLs: /ctf/xss-victim.html answers with a 308 redirect to /ctf/xss-victim . The redirected request no longer matched, received the site-wide strict policy, and the exercise's own harness script was blocked. Locally everything worked, because the local server did not redirect. The fix was to match both forms of the path: export const VICTIM_PATHS = new Set ([ " /ctf/xss-victim " , " /ctf/xss-victim.html " ]); If you assign different policies by URL, test them against production URLs, after every redirect your host performs. If you want to see what that sandboxed target is for, the reflected XSS exercise uses it: Reflected XSS lab . Making CSP violations visible Both problems became visible once the browser was asked to report them. MDN describes the modern mechanism: the report-to directive names an endpoint, and the separate Reporting-Endpoints response header maps that name to a URL. Reports arrive as POST requests with Content-Type: application/reports+json , each with "type": "csp-violation" . MDN marks report-to as Baseline 2026 (newly available) and notes that browsers which support it ignore the older report-uri . Until support is universal, MDN's own example sends both. The headers look like this: Reporting-Endpoints: csp="/api/csp-report" Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; ...; report-to csp; report-uri /api/csp-report The collector: small on purpose A violation endpoint is public by design: every visitor's browser posts to it, without a session. That makes it an input like any other. The collector Breachloom runs follows a few rules: Known content types only: application/csp-report (legacy report-uri ), application/reports+json (Reporting API) and application/json . Anything else gets 415 . Bounded body: at most 16 KB is read; malformed JSON is dropped silently. Rate limit per hashed IP , failing open, so a broken limiter never breaks the page. Allow-list of fields: document, directive, blocked URI, source file, line and a short sample. No query strings or fragments in stored URIs, because they can hold session IDs, reset tokens or e-mail addresses. No database writes: one structured log line per report. Always 204 , so the response never feeds back into the client. The two report formats differ: report-uri sends {"csp-report": {...}} with kebab-case keys, while the Reporting API sends an array of reports with camelCase keys in body . One small function normalises both: const s = ( v , n = 200 ) => typeof v === " string " ? v . slice ( 0 , n ) : "" ; const uri = v => s ( v , 300 ). replace ( / [ ?# ] .*$/ , "" ); // drop query and fragment const int = v => Number . isInteger ( v ) && v >= 0 && v < 1 e7 ? v : null ; export function pickFields ( r ) { return { doc : uri ( r [ " document-uri " ] || r . documentURL ), directive : s ( r [ " effective-directive " ] || r . effectiveDirective || r [ " violated-directive " ] || r . violatedDirective , 80 ), blocked : uri ( r [ " blocked-uri " ] || r . blockedURL ), source : uri ( r [ " source-file " ] || r . sourceFile ), line : int ( r [ " line-number " ] ?? r . lineNumber ), sample : s ( r [ " script-sample " ] || r . sample , 80 ) }; } A rollout checklist that would have caught both Start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only and the same report-to endpoint. Nothing is blocked; everything that would be blocked is reported. Read the reports grouped by directive and blocked host. A third-party host you did not add yourself, such as an injected beacon, shows up here first. Test policies on production URLs , including redirects and trailing-slash variants, if any page gets a different policy. Keep the enforcing policy and the report endpoint together. A strict policy without reporting is a silent one. Treat the collector as public input: content type, size, rate, field allow-list, no tokens in logs. For the directive-by-directive side (nonces vs hashes, strict-dynamic , frame-ancestors ), there is a longer guide: Content Security Policy: header, directives, nonces and rollout . The fastest way to feel what CSP is defending against is to break a page yourself: the free IDOR case needs no account, and the XSS exercises are part of the paid catalogue. What did your first CSP report reveal: a script you forgot, a browser extension, or something injected by your own platform? title: UI/UX in Software Development: Why It Matters and How Developers Can Build It In
author: Tamana
summary: UI/UX in software development decides whether people can actually use what you've built. The backend can be fast and the APIs clean, but if a user can't work out how to sign up or where to find their data, the product fails at the point that matters most to them. UI (user interface) is what people see and touch: buttons, forms, layouts, type. UX (user experience) is how easily they get from what they want to done. Developers shape both, because every design decision ends up as code someone has to write, test and maintain. What is the difference between UI and UX? UI is the visible, interactive layer: • Buttons, forms, menus and navigation • Colour, typography, spacing and layout • Icons and interactive states such as hover, focus and disabled UX is whether the product makes sense to the person using it. It covers understanding user needs, organising information, mapping user journeys and spotting usability problems. A quick example: a registration form can look polished and still frustrate people. If the password rules only appear after a failed submit, or the error just says "Invalid input", that's a UX problem no amount of styling will fix. Put simply, good UI makes an interface clear and consistent. Good UX makes it easy to use. Why does UI/UX matter for developers? 1. Usability problems are cheaper to fix early Think about an online learning platform. A student wants to find a course, open the materials and check their progress. If each of those takes three menus, they'll give up or flood support with questions. Spotting a confusing workflow at the wireframe stage costs a meeting. Spotting it after launch can mean rebuilding screens, routes and sometimes the data model behind them. 2. Designers and developers need each other early UI/UX isn't only the designer's job. Designers think about layouts, interactions and journeys. Developers think about component structure, technical feasibility, responsiveness and performance. Say a designer proposes a full-screen animation on page load. It looks great on a laptop and stutters on a mid-range Android phone. If a developer raises that during design review, the team can swap in a lighter CSS transition and keep the intent. Raised a week before release, it usually just gets cut. 3. Responsive design is about tasks, not just fitting the screen People move between phones, tablets and desktops all day. An interface that works perfectly on a 27-inch monitor can be a struggle on a 6-inch screen. Responsive design means: • Flexible layouts and components • Text that stays readable at every size • Touch targets big enough for a thumb • Navigation that doesn't depend on hover CSS Grid, Flexbox and media queries handle the layout side. The real test is different: can someone finish the checkout or submit the form on a small screen without zooming in or mis-tapping? 4. Accessibility starts in the markup An interface should work for people using keyboards, screen readers, magnification or voice control. Most of the groundwork is everyday front-end practice: • Use semantic HTML (header, nav, main, button). • Give every form field a visible label that's connected to the input. • Check colour contrast: WCAG asks for at least 4.5:1 for normal body text (W3C contrast guidance). • Make sure everything works with a keyboard and shows a visible focus state. The classic example is the clickable div: Submit Submit A native can be focused, responds to Enter and Space, and is announced as a button by screen readers, all without extra code (MDN's button reference covers the details). Recreating that on a div means adding tabindex, a role and key handlers, and it's easy to miss one. Accessibility added at the end is a retrofit. Built in from the first component, it costs very little. 5. Consistent components are easier to maintain As an app grows, three slightly different buttons quietly turn into twelve. A design system stops that by defining reusable pieces (buttons, inputs, navigation, cards, notifications) with agreed states and behavior. In a framework like React, each of those becomes one component. Change the focus style once and it updates everywhere. Users get predictable behavior, and developers get far less duplicate code to maintain. How can developers build UI/UX into their workflow? A practical UI/UX process starts with the problem, not with colours or code. These five steps work for most projects: Understand the users. Who is this for, what are they trying to do, and what's getting in their way? Write it down before you pick a stack. Map the user journey. List the steps for the main task. For a course website: Visit website → Explore courses → Select a course → Register → Receive confirmation. Every extra step is a chance for someone to drop off. Wireframe before you style. Low-fidelity layouts in a tool like Figma let the team agree on structure and content order while changes are still cheap. Build reusable components with all their states. Loading, empty, error, disabled and success states are where most real-world UX bugs hide. Design and build them on purpose, not as an afterthought. Test with real tasks, then refine. Ask someone who didn't build it to complete the main task on a phone. Watch where they hesitate, and fix that first. Design, build, test, refine. Then do it again. What UI/UX mistakes do developers make most often? • Styling over usability: effects that slow the page or distract from the task. • Desktop-only testing: resizing a browser window isn't the same as using a real phone. • Vague error messages: "Something went wrong" tells the user nothing. Say what happened and how to fix it. • Inconsistent components: two buttons that look the same but behave differently erode trust. • Treating accessibility as optional: if it doesn't work with a keyboard, it doesn't work for everyone. • Skipping usability testing: what's obvious to the people who built it often confuses a first-time user. Is UI/UX worth learning if you're a developer? Yes. You don't need to become a designer, but understanding user journeys, accessibility and component states makes you better at implementation, easier to work with in design reviews, and more useful on small teams where roles overlap. For front-end developers especially, it's now part of the job. Final thoughts Working code is the starting point, not the finish line. Clear navigation, accessible interactions, responsive layouts and a logical journey are what turn a functioning app into one people actually want to use. Great software isn't only about what happens behind the screen. It's about how easily people can use what's in front of them. title: AI Automation Agency vs In-House Hire: Cost, Speed and When Each Makes Sense
author: Retailbox Automation
summary: By Mikhail Oskola, founder of Retailbox Automation. Checked: salary figures as published by the trackers named in the text, dated 31 August to 3 September 2026. An AI automation agency and an in-house automation hire solve the same problem two different ways. One you pay per project or per month; the other you put on payroll and manage yourself. An agency usually costs less upfront and can start sooner, because there is no hiring step; an in-house hire costs more from day one but gives you someone embedded in the business full-time, with no vendor to coordinate once they're ramped. We're an agency, so we have a stake in this answer. Neither is the default right answer. It depends on how much ongoing automation work you actually have, and whether that work is steady enough to justify a full-time salary. This breaks down the real cost difference, when each option makes sense, and why companies past a certain size often end up running both at once. Agency vs. in-house hire: what's actually different? An AI automation agency is a team you hire per project or on a monthly retainer. A good one has built workflows like yours before for other companies; check that in its references, not in its pitch. The catch: you're sharing their attention with other clients, and the relationship ends, or continues on a retainer, when the project does. An in-house automation hire is one person (or a small team) on your payroll, full-time, sitting in your meetings and your Slack. They know your business, your data, and your stack better than any outside team ever will. But they cost a full salary whether there's automation work that week or not, and if they leave, most of what they knew leaves with them unless it was documented. Neither option is automatically cheaper or more serious than the other. The right call depends on how much steady automation work actually exists, not on which one sounds more permanent. What's the real cost difference? Agency (project-based) In-house hire (full-time) Upfront cost A project fee per build; our current ranges are on our AI automation agency page $0 upfront - but a full salary starts the day they're hired Time to first working automation 1-2 weeks for a quick automation, 3-8 for a CRM build, 6-16 for a custom AI system Weeks to months, plus time to hire, then ramp on your stack Ongoing cost if work is steady A monthly managed-support plan, or a new project fee per initiative About $134,000-$168,000/year fully loaded - base salary plus 25-40% for benefits and overhead Cost in a month with no automation work Nothing beyond an existing managed plan Full salary, same as any other month What happens if the relationship ends Depends on the contract: ask for documentation and admin access as part of the handoff. The people who built it leave Everything they knew walks out with them, unless it was written down The row that actually decides this for most companies is the third one: whether there's enough steady automation work to keep one full-time person busy all year. A single CRM migration or one automation project doesn't clear that bar. An agency finishes it and moves on, and you're not carrying a salary through the months between initiatives. A company running dozens of workflows that need constant tuning, new integrations as tools get added, and someone who can drop everything when one breaks starts looking more like a full-time job. When does an in-house hire or AI team make sense? An in-house automation hire earns their salary once there's enough automation and integration work to fill a full-time role year-round. Not one project, but a continuous backlog: new integrations as the company adds tools, workflows that need rebuilding as the business changes, and enough volume that someone sitting in daily standups catches problems before they get expensive. It also makes sense when the work touches something sensitive enough that having it built by someone who reports to you, not a vendor, is worth the premium: regulated data, or a process nobody outside the company should see the internals of. The tradeoff is ramp time: even a strong senior hire needs weeks to learn your CRM, your data model, and which systems are actually load-bearing before they ship anything real. When does an agency or specialist consultancy make more sense? An agency makes more sense when the automation need is real but doesn't add up to a full-time job: one CRM implementation, a handful of workflows, an AI agent for one specific process. If the agency has built something similar before, it isn't learning on your time, and you're not carrying a six-figure salary through the months when there's nothing to build. It's also the lower-risk starting point if you're not sure automation will be a permanent function in the company yet. Run one project, see the payback, and decide whether it's worth building a team around before committing to a hire. Can an agency work alongside an in-house ops person? Yes, and it's a common setup past a certain size. An in-house ops or RevOps person who owns the day-to-day and knows the business, backed by an agency for the specialized builds a generalist can't take on alone (a CRM migration, an AI agent, anything outside what one person can build and still do their regular job). The in-house person doesn't need to be a full automation engineer to make this work; they need to know what's running, flag what's breaking, and be the point of contact when an outside project needs internal context. What does an in-house automation hire actually cost? US automation engineer salaries sit in a fairly tight band across the major trackers. As of September 2026: Salary.com puts the national average at $108,677 (as of September 1, 2026), Indeed at $108,033 (updated August 31, 2026), ZipRecruiter at $107,126 (as of September 3, 2026), and Glassdoor higher at $119,731. Built In puts engineers with 7+ years of experience at $131,421 on average. One caveat on all of these: "automation engineer" is a broad job title. The same salary data also covers QA test-automation engineers and industrial or manufacturing automation roles, so it's a reasonable benchmark for a business-process automation hire, not an exact match. None of those figures is the full cost. Benefits and payroll overhead are commonly estimated at another 25-40% on top of base salary. Applied to the $107,000-$120,000 base range above, that puts a fully loaded in-house automation hire at about $134,000-$168,000 a year, before they've shipped a single workflow. For the agency side, the only seller's numbers we can vouch for are our own, published on our AI automation agency page . Read them as one data point and get quotes from other agencies too. Rough breakeven: a $150,000/year fully loaded hire costs about $12,500 a month whether there's work that month or not. If there's enough steady automation work to keep one person building or maintaining something every month, the salary is the better buy. If there isn't, project work costs less. title: Building an annotation-driven MCP server in Java
author: Ayush Soni
summary: Exposing a Java method to an AI agent should take one annotation. When I started using MCP servers daily with Claude Code and Cursor, I noticed that almost every example was written in Python or TypeScript — while most of the systems I'd want an agent to call are Spring Boot services. So I wrote java-mcp-server : a small toolkit where this is the whole integration: @Component public class MyTools { @McpTool ( name = "greet" , description = "Say hello to someone" ) public String greet ( @McpParam ( value = "name" , description = "Person's name" ) String name ) { return "Hello, " + name + "!" ; } @McpResource ( uri = "config://app/{key}" , description = "Read a config value" ) public String config ( @McpParam ( "key" ) String key ) { return System . getProperty ( key , "(not set)" ); } } Start the app, and any MCP client can list and call greet and read config://app/java.version . This post covers how it works, the decisions behind it, and the parts I'd change. MCP in one paragraph The Model Context Protocol is a JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol between an AI client (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor) and a server that offers tools (functions the model may call), resources (read-only data addressed by URI) and prompts. A session starts with initialize , the client asks tools/list , and when the model decides to use a tool the client sends tools/call with a name and JSON arguments. That's the core loop — and it maps almost one-to-one onto "find a method, describe it, invoke it". The shape of the toolkit I split the project into four Maven modules, and the split turned out to be the most useful decision in the project: Module What it holds Depends on Spring? mcp-core Annotations ( @McpTool , @McpResource , @McpParam ) and the JSON-RPC / tool models No mcp-server-spring-boot Auto-configuration, bean scanning, the /mcp HTTP endpoint Yes mcp-server-stdio Newline-delimited JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout, for Claude Desktop No mcp-server-sample A runnable app with system-info and math tools Yes Keeping mcp-core free of Spring meant the stdio transport — which Claude Desktop uses when it launches a server as a child process — was a small module on top of the same models, not a second implementation. One endpoint, two registries, plain Spring beans underneath. Explore the interactive diagram Step 1: turn methods into tool definitions At startup, McpToolRegistry walks every bean in the ApplicationContext , looks for methods carrying @McpTool , and builds a ToolDefinition for each one. The interesting part is the input schema, because that's what the model reads to decide how to call your method: for ( Parameter param : method . getParameters ()) { McpParam mp = param . getAnnotation ( McpParam . class ); String paramName = mp != null ? mp . value () : param . getName (); String paramDesc = mp != null ? mp . description () : "" ; boolean isRequired = mp == null || mp . required (); properties . put ( paramName , new ParameterSchema ( jsonType ( param . getType ()), paramDesc )); if ( isRequired ) required . add ( paramName ); } Java types map to JSON Schema types ( int / long → integer , double → number , boolean → boolean , everything else → string ). It's deliberately simple. I found that descriptions matter more than types : a model given name: string guesses; a model given "Person's name, as it should appear in the greeting" gets it right. Step 2: one endpoint, a switch on the method Every request arrives at a single POST /mcp (configurable via mcp.endpoint ). The controller is a switch over the JSON-RPC method: return switch ( method ) { case "initialize" -> handleInitialize ( id ); case "tools/list" -> handleToolsList ( id ); case "tools/call" -> handleToolsCall ( id , request . getParams ()); case "resources/list" -> handleResourcesList ( id ); case "resources/read" -> handleResourcesRead ( id , request . getParams ()); case "notifications/initialized" , "notifications/cancelled" -> JsonRpcResponse . success ( id , null ); default -> JsonRpcResponse . error ( id , ERR_METHOD_NOT_FOUND , "Unknown method: " + method ); }; Errors use the JSON-RPC codes clients expect: -32601 for an unknown method, -32602 for bad params (a missing tool name, an unknown tool, a URI that matches no resource), -32603 for anything that blew up inside. Step 3: invoke, and never throw at the model McpToolInvoker maps each JSON argument onto the Java parameter type with Jackson's treeToValue , calls the method reflectively, and wraps the return value: strings pass through, anything else is serialised to JSON. The rule I settled on: a failing tool returns a tool error, not a protocol error. If your method throws, the client receives a ToolResult flagged as an error with the cause's message. The model can read that and recover ("the divisor can't be zero, let me ask the user"), which it can't do with a transport-level failure. Resources: a tiny URI-template matcher @McpResource(uri = "config://app/{key}") registers a template. When a client reads config://app/java.version , the registry splits both on / , matches literal segments, and captures {variables} into a map that's passed to the method. It's twenty lines and handles the common cases; it doesn't do wildcards or query strings, and I haven't needed them yet. Two transports, one handler HTTP is the natural fit for a service already running in your infrastructure. Claude Desktop, though, launches MCP servers as child processes and speaks newline-delimited JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout. McpStdioRunner is a read-line loop around the same request handler, with two details that bit me: Logs must go to stderr. Anything written to stdout that isn't a JSON-RPC message corrupts the stream. Notifications get no response. A message without an id must not produce a reply, or strict clients drop the connection. What I'd do differently This is a v0.1, and three things are already on my list: Proxied beans hide annotations. The registry reads bean.getClass().getMethods() . If the bean is wrapped in a CGLIB proxy — say because it has @Transactional — the proxy's overriding methods don't carry @McpTool , and the tool silently disappears. The fix is to resolve the target class with AopUtils.getTargetClass() and use AnnotationUtils.findAnnotation . Missing arguments become null . That's fine for String , but a missing value for an int parameter fails at invoke time. Validate against the required list before calling and return a clear -32602 . Parameter names need -parameters . Without @McpParam , names come from reflection, which yields arg0 unless the code is compiled with the -parameters flag. Either fail fast at startup or require @McpParam . Takeaways Keep the protocol core independent of your framework; transports become cheap. Spend your effort on descriptions and schemas — that's the interface the model actually reads. Return tool failures as data the model can reason about. The code, tests and sample app are on GitHub . If you're putting internal Java services in front of agents, I'd like to hear how you're handling auth — that's the next big piece. Originally published at ayushwing.com .

title: How Claude Code and Codex Decide Which Skill Descriptions the Model Reads
author: Mayur Agnani
summary: Engineer's view. This is a cache that evicts the least-used entry. A key you just added has the lowest hit count, so it goes first, and it never earns the hits that would keep it. Claude Code trims its skill list the same way. A skill you installed today is the first to lose its description. TL;DR. A coding agent shows the model only a short list of your skills, and that list has a size limit. Past the limit, descriptions get cut, and a skill the model cannot read about is a skill it rarely picks. Explain Like I'm 5 A school has one small board by the door. Every club pins a card with its name and what it does. Kids read the board to decide where to go after lunch. Then too many clubs sign up. The teacher keeps every name on the board but crosses out the descriptions of the clubs that got the fewest visitors lately. A brand-new club has had no visitors yet, so its description is crossed out first. A kid who loves chess walks past a card that just says "Knights". Nothing tells them it is the chess club. So the new club stays empty, and its card stays crossed out. The Problem You have shipped this bug already, in a system with no model in it. Your service wrote one log line per request. Someone added a field near the front, and the line crossed the log shipper's size limit. The shipper did not fail. It cut each line at the limit and sent the rest. The request ID sat at the end of the line, so searching by request ID stopped finding anything. No alert fired, because every line still arrived. The bug was not in any one field. It was a shared size limit, plus a rule for what gets cut when the limit is hit. Adding something new quietly took words away from something old. A skill in a coding agent has the same bug. A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file: a name, a description, and instructions for one kind of task. Coding agents that support the open Agent Skills format do not load your skills up front. They show the model a skill listing : each skill's name and description, and nothing else. The model reads that listing and decides which skill fits your request. The listing has a size limit, a fixed share of the context window , the model's working memory for the session. Install enough skills, and the listing overflows. Each tool then cuts it by its own rule. A skill whose description was cut can still be listed and still never be chosen. The fix: keep the listing under its budget, put each skill's use case in its first sentence and its name, and check what the model actually sees. The Fix: Keep the Listing Under Budget and Put the Use Case First What does the model actually see? Agent Skills loads in three steps, which the spec calls progressive disclosure . At the start of a session the model sees only the listing. When a request matches a description, it reads that skill's full SKILL.md . Scripts and reference files load only when the instructions point at them. So the description does all of the choosing. There is no keyword matcher behind it. The model reads the words and makes a judgment. How big is the listing allowed to be? Claude Code gives it 1% of the context window. Codex gives it 2%, or 8,000 characters when the window size is unknown. On a 200K-token model, 1% is about 8,000 characters, at roughly four characters per token. That is not much. The 41 skills on the machine this article was written on have a median description of 408 characters. About eighteen such skills fill Claude Code's listing. What gets cut when it overflows? The two tools use different rules. Claude Code keeps every name. It drops whole descriptions, starting with the skills you invoke least. Codex shortens descriptions first and omits whole skills only for very large sets. Why does a brand-new skill go quiet first? Under Claude Code's rule, a skill you installed today has zero invocations. It is first in line to lose its description. The model then sees only its name, picks it less, and its count stays at zero. Unless you invoke it by hand, it never climbs out. What This Means for You When this matters. You have more than about twenty skills, counting the ones that plugins bring along. Or you switch between a 1M-token model and a smaller one. The budget is a share of the window, so a smaller window shrinks it. A skill that worked yesterday can lose its description when you change models. How it affects you. The failure is quiet. The skill still shows up in the / menu, and it still works when you type its name. What stops is the model choosing it on its own. You notice weeks later, when a review skips the checklist you wrote for it. In Claude Code the newest skills are hit first. In Codex every description gets shorter, so a description that saves its trigger words for the last sentence loses exactly those words. What to do about it. Start with one minute and no new tooling. In Claude Code, run /context and read the Skills row. It shows the listing's size after the budget is applied. If it sits near 1% of your window, you are at the edge. Then open your three newest skills and read the first sentence of each description. If it does not say when to use the skill, rewrite it so it does. Then make it a habit. Turn off skills you never use, set manual-only skills so they leave the listing, and add a size check to the repo that holds your team's skills. ## Implementing It shows all three. Implementing It The change. Three people touch this, and each change is small. Role 1, whoever writes the skill. Put the use case first, and make the name carry it too. A name survives every cut that a description does not. Keep the whole description short enough that a cut at about 250 characters still leaves the trigger. # before: the trigger is in the last sentence, and the name says nothing name : notes description : Collects merged pull requests, groups them by area, and drafts a summary for customers in the house style. ... Use when the user asks for release notes. # after: the trigger leads, and the name alone still says what it is for name : release-notes description : Use when the user asks for release notes or a changelog for customers. Groups merged pull requests by area in the house style. In the demo, the Codex cut keeps 244 characters per description once a plugin doubles the skill count. The "before" description loses the words "release notes". The "after" keeps them. Role 2, whoever owns the agent setup. Remove what the model never needs to choose. A skill you only run by hand should leave the listing entirely. In its frontmatter, Claude Code reads disable-model-invocation: true . Codex reads allow_implicit_invocation: false under policy in agents/openai.yaml . For skills you cannot edit, use .claude/settings.json in Claude Code and ~/.codex/config.toml in Codex: { "skillOverrides" : { "legacy-context" : "name-only" , "old-deploy" : "off" } } # ~/.codex/config.toml [[ skills . config ]] path = "/Users/you/.agents/skills/old-deploy" enabled = false You can also raise the budget. In Claude Code, set skillListingBudgetFraction (for example 0.02 ). In Codex, set skills.max_context_tokens , up to 10,000 tokens. Every character you add is paid on every turn, so prune first. Role 3, whoever owns the repo that ships the team's skills. Fail the build when the listing would overflow on the smallest model your team uses. read_skills and claude_code_listing in code_example.py do the parsing and the arithmetic: skills = read_skills ([ " .claude/skills " , " .agents/skills " ]) shown , budget = claude_code_listing ( skills , context_tokens = 200_000 ) dropped = [ name for name , desc in shown . items () if not desc ] assert not dropped , f " over the { budget } -char listing budget: { dropped } " How you know it worked. In Claude Code, the Skills row in /context should drop below the budget, and --debug should stop logging the overflow warning. /skill-doctor lists skills that were never invoked, with what each costs. In Codex, the warning about omitted skills should go away. Then check the behavior, not just the size. Pick five requests that should trigger the new skill. Run each in a fresh session with claude -p "<request>" --output-format json , and look for a Skill tool call naming it. Most of the five should now load the skill. When Trimming the Listing Is the Wrong Tool When you have a handful of skills. Ten skills with 400-character descriptions fit with room to spare. Rewriting them buys nothing. When the rule must hold every time. A skill is advice the model can skip, even when it was loaded. If every edit must pass a check, put the check in a hook. Claude Code's own docs say the same. When the listing is not the problem. A skill can be listed in full and still not be chosen. The model tends to skip skills for tasks it can do alone, like reading one file. That is a description problem, and no budget change will fix it. And raising the budget is not free. The listing is read on every turn. Doubling it on a big team costs context that every session pays for. Three questions before you change anything: Does /context show the Skills row near its budget on the smallest model you use? Do your newest skills say when to use them in the first sentence, and in the name? Which of your skills are only ever run by hand, and still listed for the model? Glossary skill — a folder with a SKILL.md file: a name, a description, and instructions for one kind of task. skill listing — the names and descriptions the model sees at the start of a session. context window — the model's working memory for a session, measured in tokens. progressive disclosure — loading the listing first, a skill's instructions on a match, and its files only when needed. invoke — run a skill, either because the model chose it or because you typed its name. Further reading How to add skills support to your agent — Agent Skills specification site (format originated by Anthropic) Extend Claude with skills — Anthropic, Claude Code docs Build skills — OpenAI, Codex docs Optimizing skill descriptions — Agent Skills specification site Originally published at theaicommit.com , a daily AI engineering lab for software engineers. The original has an interactive version you can play with, and the full runnable code is on GitHub .

title: I Joined an AI Competition With 7 Days Left. 940 Teams Had the Same Score.
author: Marvin Okafor
summary: So I went sideways instead. Here is what happened, and what a week spent teaching a computer to read knee scans taught me about work that has nothing to do with medicine. The setup A global medical imaging society ran an open competition. The task: build software that looks at an MRI scan of a knee and flags twelve common problems. Torn ligaments, torn cartilage, arthritis, fluid on the knee, fractures, that sort of thing. About 25,700 people entered, in roughly 6,000 teams, over two months. I joined with seven days left, working alone, on the free cloud computers Kaggle hands out each week. Total spend: nothing. Total compute: about six hours. Then I looked at the leaderboard and found something strange. Around 940 teams were sitting at exactly the same score. Not similar. Identical. They had all downloaded the same publicly shared solution and run it unchanged. Catching the actual leaders in seven days, alone, was not going to happen. But the competition had a second prize, for models that are both accurate and fast, and almost none of those 940 copied solutions were fast. That is where I went. Where I ended up My model scores 0.919 on the public leaderboard and reads the whole test set of roughly 1,300 knee scans in about nine minutes. Under half a second per scan. The popular public solution took a few hours for the same job. What does 0.919 mean in plain English? Show the model two knees, one with a given problem and one without. About 92 times out of 100 it rates the problem knee as the more suspicious of the pair. It is a ranking measure, not a diagnosis. The leading models score around 0.96. So I am a few points behind them, running in minutes instead of hours. Whether that wins anything is not settled yet. The week was worth it regardless, because almost everything I learned transfers. Lesson 1: the most valuable data is usually the notes you already wrote Here is the part that surprised me most. The training set had about 4,400 knee scans. Only 58 of them had been properly labelled by expert radiologists. Fifty-eight. That is nowhere near enough to teach a computer anything. But every single scan came with something else: the radiologist's written report. The actual notes a doctor typed after looking at it. In several different languages, because the data came from more than twenty hospitals across Europe, the Americas, Asia, Africa and Australia. People in the competition community wrote code to turn those free-text reports into usable yes/no labels for each condition, and published the results. I combined fifteen of those label sets into one. A dataset of 58 became a dataset of 4,400, and it came out of writing that already existed. The lesson: your organisation is sitting on years of emails, case notes, support tickets, incident reports and meeting minutes. That messy pile of text is very often the dataset you have been telling yourself you do not have. You do not need to re-interview every customer if you already have a decade of their complaints. Lesson 2: when everyone copies the same answer, change the question Nine hundred and forty teams at an identical score is not a competition. It is a queue. Fighting for a fractional improvement at the front of that queue, with seven days and one person, was hopeless. But the organisers had quietly set a second scoring rule, one almost nobody in the queue was optimising for. The lesson: in a crowded market, the opening is rarely a better version of what everyone else is doing. It is usually a different definition of winning. Look for the scoring rule nobody is playing by. Lesson 3: "good enough now" often beats "perfect eventually" A model that is slightly less accurate but reads a scan in half a second can sort an entire morning's queue before the radiologist has finished their coffee. The likely fracture goes to the top of the pile. The routine follow-up goes to the bottom. A near-perfect model that takes hours cannot do that job at all. Think of a triage nurse. Their job is not to diagnose every patient correctly. It is to make sure the most urgent person is seen first, quickly. Different job, different tool. The competition actually priced this trade-off into its formula: one hundredth of extra accuracy was worth about eleven and a half minutes of runtime. I think being forced to state that exchange rate out loud is a useful exercise for any organisation. The lesson: before optimising anything, ask what the output is for. Sorting a queue and making a final call are not the same requirement. Lesson 4: the slow part is almost never the clever part I assumed the AI would be the bottleneck. It is the complicated bit, so it must be the slow bit. The AI took 0.07 seconds per scan. The rest of the nine minutes went on opening files. Over 800,000 individual image files, each with a small block of information attached describing what it is and where in the knee it sits. Just reading those well enough to put the slices in the right order was the real cost. Reading only the four pieces of information I actually needed, instead of everything, and opening many files at once instead of one after another, is where the speed came from. None of that is clever. All of it mattered. The lesson: measure before you optimise, because your intuition about where the time goes is probably wrong. In most organisations the delay is not the expert's decision. It is the paperwork wrapped around the decision. Lesson 5: adding more opinions can make things worse Near the end I blended my model with the strong public solution, expecting the combination to beat either one alone. That is usually how this works. The score went down. From 0.956 to 0.952. A noticeably weaker voice added to a strong panel did not add balance. It added noise. The lesson: adding people to a decision helps when they bring something the group lacks, at a comparable standard. A weaker duplicate of an opinion already in the room makes the room worse, not more democratic. Lesson 6: small tests lie, and they lie confidently With only 58 expertly labelled scans to check against, any score I measured on them could be off by around three points in either direction. Most of the improvements I was testing were smaller than that. So the test could not tell me whether my changes worked. I relied on a rougher but much larger check across all 4,400 scans instead. The lesson: do not judge a new hire on one week, a campaign on one day, or a supplier on one order. A small sample gives you a clear, confident, meaningless answer. Lesson 7: being able to defend your work beats a better number Several popular solutions used outside medical datasets whose licence terms were unclear for this competition. Using them would almost certainly have raised my score. I built only from the competition's own data and from starting points with clear open licences, and kept a record of where everything came from. That cost me points. The lesson: in healthcare, finance, law or anything regulated, where your data came from is part of the product. A lower number you can defend beats a higher one you cannot. Why any of this matters The knee is the most commonly injured and imaged joint in the body. Osteoarthritis alone affects an estimated 654 million people, and acute knee injuries are somewhere between 15 and 40 percent of all sports injuries. Specialist musculoskeletal radiologists are scarce, much more so outside major cities and wealthy countries. Scans wait. Readings vary between doctors. A tool that reads a scan in under a second on modest hardware is the kind that can actually be deployed in a hospital with one radiologist and a long queue. The heaviest, most accurate model in the world is no use if nobody there can run it. An important caveat. This is a research competition model. It is not a medical device, it has not been clinically validated, and it does not diagnose anything. At best it helps an expert decide what to look at first. The part worth repeating A week, one person, free computers, open-source tools, and a community that published its working. Ten years ago this needed a funded lab. The barrier is no longer access to the tools. It is clear thinking about which problem to solve, and what "good" means for the person who has to use the result. I could not have done this in seven days without the labels and tooling other competitors published for free. I have published my code, models and notebook in return.
